comments.author: @AvidGardener5D
comments.text: My tip is, never be a tourist, always be a local.  Don't talk to anyone you don't know on the street. Know where you are going by researching ahead of time.  Pay in cash.  Don't walk around looking bewildered. Look determined, like you have a goal in mind.  If you have to stop, don't stop in the middle of the street, stop somewhere where there's a wall behind you so you can look at your phone or whatever without giving someone an opportunity to take you by surprise. Don't clutch tourist articles, put them in your bag.  You're a local, remember?  Stay sober in public.   I've lived in major cities and traveled around the world and this has always served me well.

That's why you're here too I'm assuming. That's why you're watching Cal's video too. You already have one up on the scammers. You're aware of these situations. Stay away from over 50cc bikes if you are from the States. Even with an IDL and motorcycle endorsement, Vietnam technically does NOT recognize it, as they only recognize the treaty in the 60's, and the States' one is from the 1940's. You can still get fined, and have it confiscated if they stop you. Look it up if you do not believe.

They will still most likely rent you one, but it is still illegal on your part to ride it. Ride at your own risk though...

comments.text:
Thanks Cal. I'm going to Asia next year, definitely going to hit Bangkok, Pattaya, and Hong Kong. Thought about Vietnam. I may or may not go. It depends on my timing, but this was informative. 

It's really nothing different than any other developing country: same scams, different faces, different language, that's all.

All those people who are being turned off by traveling to Vietnam, you're going to face the same in every country. First world countries, third world countries. If you're a savvy and wary traveler, you'll see it coming from a mile away. It's up to you how vulnerable you are.

The best thing about most Asian countries is there's not really any violence. You're not getting straight up robbed. You're being tricked. Being tricked is on you. Being strong-armed is a different thing entirely and that very rarely happens in most Asian countries.

People are completely misinterpreting Cal’s video and confusing opportunistic hassle with actual danger. Every region in the world has a tourist tax; you just need to understand what kind of tax you are dealing with. 

There is a huge  difference between strong-arm crime and cons/scams, and understanding this distinction is the difference between traveling safely and staying home out of irrational fear.

1. The High-Risk Zone: Strong-Arm Crime (The Caribbean / Parts of Latin America)In places with high rates of violent crime, like parts of Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, or various major hubs in the Americas, crime is often predatory and physical (strong-arm). 

This means armed robberies, physical muggings, or targeted smash-and-grabs.
The Tactic: Criminals leverage physical dominance, weapons, and environmental isolation to force compliance.The Reality: If you get cornered in a bad neighborhood or set up by a predatory taxi driver in these zones, spatial awareness won't save you. 

You cannot outsmart a gun or a blade. Your only defensive move is compliance—handing over your wallet and hoping you don't get hurt.

2. The Low-Violent Zone: Psychological Exploitation (Vietnam, Thailand, Egypt) 
By contrast, violent crime against tourists in Southeast Asia or Egypt is statistically incredibly rare. Instead, you face hyper-aggressive opportunism and psychological traps.

The Tactic: These scammers weaponize your own psychology against you. They exploit your politeness, your desire to avoid a public scene, your lack of spatial awareness, and your ignorance of local currency/pricing.

The Reality: An Egyptian vendor placing a "free gift" in your hand or the pyramids are closed and only they can grant you access or give you a ride around on a camel for a ridiculous price that you didn't negotiate beforehand, or a Vietnamese restaurant pulling a "switcheroo menu" isn’t trying to assault you. 

They are playing a high-pressure mental game, betting that you will pay a fake $40 bill just to escape the social awkwardness.

The Golden Rule: Scams are 95% Preventable

You cannot outthink a violent strong-arm mugger, but you can absolutely outsmart a scammer. 

In Asia, your safety is rarely at risk, but your wallet always is—meaning the power is entirely in your hands. You can completely avoid paying the "scam tax" by being hyper-aware and proactive:

Audit the Paper Trail: Take photos of the menu and prices before you order. If they bring a duplicate menu with jacked-up prices at the end of the meal, you have digital receipts to kill the argument instantly.

Kill the Cash Flash: Do not walk around with large rolls of cash or flashy gold jewelry. No one in Hanoi or Bangkok is impressed by a Rolex, but it does signal to pickpockets that you are a high-value, low-awareness target.

Lock Down Your Identity: Leave your physical passport locked securely in your hotel room. Carry a Xerox copy or a digital scan on your phone for daily use.

Bypass the Street Hustle: Never flag down random street taxis or tuk-tuks. Use localized apps like Grab where the route is GPS-tracked, the driver is identified, and the price is locked before you even step inside.Stop letting Cal’s video scare you out of traveling. 

Western Europe has pickpockets, the Caribbean has strong-arm crime, and Asia has scammers. The beautiful thing about an Asian scam is that if you do an hour of research, keep your wits about you, and shed your fear of being impolite, you are effectively untouchable.

I wanted to add that I live in Times Square, 42nd and 9th Avenue, and I see the scammers every day. I have a family friend who's an undercover cop and literally all he does is walk around and let people pickpocket him. He's in disguise sort of and arrests people daily doing that.

Then I see people who get scammed by the rickshaw drivers or they don't realize the price, how much it is. Some of them, you go around the block and it's $150 and you can't argue it. They'll put the price clearly marked on the side of their cart of the rickshaw and people don't really pay attention that it's $2.50 a minute or $5 a minute or more.

Or the people dressed up as your favorite Marvel characters or a giant gorilla, a Transformer, you give them your phone to take a picture. Unless you give them $5 or more, they won't give you your phone back. If you just happen to take a picture near them or maybe of them, they will insist that you give them money. They will literally try to intimidate you and they will surround you because they got each other's backs. They won't let off until they either see the police coming or you give them money.

Never give them your cell phone to take a picture. Never do that.
